title: $11 Flea Market Game Boy Advance: Full Restore + Backlit Screen
creator: Dex Rewires
description:
This GBA "turns on sometimes". Let's fix that.

Parts used:
IPS backlight kit + clear purple shell
Replacement power switch

Timestamps
0:00 The patient
0:40 Corrosion cleanup
1:30 Power switch
2:10 IPS screen install
3:20 Testing

My repair bench tour: https://youtube.com/watch?v=dexbench01

sentences.t: So this Game Boy Advance came to me for eleven dollars at a flea market, and the seller was very honest about it.
He said, quote, it turns on sometimes.
Which, in my experience, means it does not turn on.
Let's crack it open and see what we're working with.
First problem, these are tri-wing screws, so you need the little Y-shaped bit, because a normal Phillips will just strip them.
Okay, back shell's off.
And yeah, look at that, there's corrosion on the battery terminals, that green crusty stuff.
Somebody left double A's in here for probably fifteen years.
That's actually really common, and it's usually fixable.
I'm going to scrub the contacts with some isopropyl and an old toothbrush.
For the really stubborn bits, a little white vinegar on a cotton swab breaks it down.
Then rinse that with isopropyl again so you don't leave any acid behind.
Now while the board is out, let's look at the power switch.
These switches get gunked up, and that's what gives you the turns on sometimes problem.
Normally I'd hit it with some contact cleaner and flick it back and forth like twenty times.
But on this one I'm just going to replace it, they're like a dollar.
Desoldering the old one, a bit of flux, and some solder wick.
Okay, new switch in.
Now the fun part.
The original screen on these has no backlight, which is why everyone remembers playing Pokemon under a desk lamp.
So we're putting in an IPS backlit panel.
These kits come with a new screen, a ribbon cable, and usually a new shell, because the old one needs trimming.
I'm going with a new shell, a clear purple one, because I have no self-control.
The ribbon connects here, and you have to be gentle, these little latches snap if you even look at them wrong.
There's also one wire you solder to the board for the brightness control.
Mine goes to the L button pad, so I'll be able to hold select and press L to cycle the brightness.
Okay, solder's on, that's a decent joint, nice and shiny.
Screen goes in the shell, with a bit of the included adhesive to hold it.
Board goes in, then the buttons, the membranes, and we close it up.
Moment of truth.
Fresh batteries in, power on.
And there's the logo!
That's so much brighter than I expected.
Let's test brightness, select plus L.
Yep, five levels, and the highest one is honestly blinding.
I tested all the buttons and the speaker, and it all works.
So total cost on this one was about fifty-five dollars including the screen kit.
Not bad for a console that, quote, turns on sometimes.
That's going to wrap it up for this one.
Thanks for watching, and if you've got a busted handheld in a drawer somewhere, drop it in the comments and maybe I'll do it next.
See you in the next one.
